title: When would you choose vertical scaling over horizontal scaling?
summary: Tests whether you treat "always scale horizontally" as a reflex or know the real cases — a monolithic DB primary, a stateful in-memory workload — where a bigger box is genuinely the right call first.

slides.markdown:
"Horizontal scaling is always better" is a reflex many candidates memorize without the caveat — this question checks whether you know the real cases where a bigger box is genuinely the right first move, not a lesser one.

By the end of this topic you'll be able to name when vertical scaling is the correct answer, where it eventually breaks, and how to recognize the moment you should stop resizing and start sharding instead.

slides.sectionTitle: Clarifying questions: is the bottleneck a single stateful component or a stateless fleet?
slides.markdown:
Ask: is the thing that's struggling a **single stateful component** (a database primary, an in-memory cache holding a large dataset) or **a stateless fleet** (app servers behind a load balancer)?

This single question usually settles the answer — stateful, hard-to-split components are exactly where vertical scaling shines, while a stateless fleet almost never has a good reason to stay on fewer, bigger boxes instead of more, smaller ones.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: vertical first when sharding is premature, horizontal once you outgrow the biggest box
slides.markdown:
The skeleton: choose **vertical scaling first** when sharding or distributing the component would be genuinely expensive or premature relative to the problem's actual size. Switch to **horizontal scaling** once you've outgrown the biggest available instance type, or once a single box's failure is no longer an acceptable risk.

This isn't "horizontal is better" vs "vertical is better" — it's sequencing: buy time cheaply with vertical scaling, then invest in horizontal complexity only once the numbers actually demand it.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a DB primary hitting CPU limits
slides.markdown:
A database primary pegged at high CPU is the classic vertical-first case: **resizing the instance** (more cores, more RAM) is a config change and a brief restart, versus **sharding**, which means picking a shard key, migrating data, and rewriting every cross-shard query pattern — weeks of engineering work for a problem a bigger box might solve for months.

The interview signal here is sequencing: propose the resize first, and only reach for sharding once you've named why resizing won't be enough.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: the ceiling vertical scaling eventually hits
slides.markdown:
Vertical scaling isn't unlimited: there's a **biggest instance type available** from any cloud provider, and past that, there's nowhere bigger to go. There's also a **cost curve** that isn't linear — the largest instance types often cost disproportionately more per unit of CPU/RAM than a mid-sized one, since you're paying for scarcity at the top of the lineup.

Naming both the hard ceiling and the steepening cost curve shows you're not treating vertical scaling as a free, unlimited lever.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a worked resize example
slides.markdown:
A database primary is CPU-bound at 8 cores. Resizing to 32 cores:

```
Cost of resize:        ~1 config change + a few minutes of downtime for the restart
Expected runway:       12-18 months at current growth rate
Cost of sharding instead: weeks of engineering (shard key design, data migration,
                          query rewrites) for a comparable amount of headroom
```

The resize is a fraction of a sharding project's cost for a similar amount of runway — which is exactly why it's worth proposing first, even though it's the less "impressive"-sounding answer in an interview.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud: simple and consistent, until the ceiling hits all at once
slides.markdown:
| | Vertical scaling | Horizontal scaling |
|---|---|---|
| Consistency | Trivial — one copy of the data | Harder — multiple copies to keep in sync |
| Operational complexity | Low — no distributed-systems concerns | Higher — sharding, routing, rebalancing |
| Failure mode | Fine until the ceiling, then a hard stop and a scramble | Gradual — capacity grows steadily, no single wall |

**How to decide:** vertical scaling is simpler and keeps consistency easy right up until you hit the ceiling — then you pay for a sharding project all at once, under pressure, rather than having built it in gradually.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: you've resized three times already — when do you stop and shard?
slides.markdown:
The honest signal to switch: when you're **within one or two resizes of the largest instance type available**, or when the growth rate means the next resize buys less runway than the last one did (diminishing returns as you approach the ceiling).

Waiting until you're actually stuck on the biggest box, with no time to plan a migration, is the failure mode — the right moment to start a sharding project is a resize or two *before* you hit the wall, while you still have runway to do it deliberately.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: does this apply to the app tier too?
slides.markdown:
Rarely, and it's worth saying so. A **stateless app tier** rarely benefits from vertical scaling the way a database does — since it can already scale horizontally cheaply (no sharding, no data migration, just more identical nodes behind a load balancer), there's little reason to buy a bigger box instead of just adding more of the same small ones.

Vertical scaling's advantage is specifically about *avoiding the cost of distributing state* — and a stateless service was never paying that cost in the first place.

**Wrong belief:** shard the database early, since it's the "proper" scalable answer and it's better to be safe.

**Why it's wrong:** sharding adds real, permanent complexity — cross-shard queries, rebalancing, a harder consistency story — for a scaling problem a bigger instance might not have needed solving for another year or more. Premature sharding is engineering effort spent on a problem you don't have yet, at the cost of the problems you do have.

**Correct model:** resize first when the numbers support it, and shard only once you can point to specifically why resizing won't buy enough runway. See [scalability fundamentals](scalability-fundamentals) for the vertical vs horizontal vocabulary this builds on.
